questions.question: Which substitution most effectively simplifies the definite integral?

moves.name: u = x+4
moves.professor: A clean linear shift. x = u-4, the root becomes √u, and the integrand turns into a simple polynomial. One precise strike fells the enemy.

moves.name: u = x-1
moves.professor: That leaves √(u+5) nested inside. You've traded one mess for another. The enemy saw that fumble and counterattacked.

moves.name: u = √(x+4)
moves.professor: That will work — u² = x+4 gives a rational function after some algebra. It's a heavier blade, but it still cuts through.

questions.question: Set up the integral using the washer method for the volume when the region bounded by the curves below is revolved about the x-axis.

moves.name: V = π ∫_{-1}^{0} [(x^3)^2 - (-x^2)^2] dx
moves.professor: On [-1,0], x^3 sits above -x^2. Outer radius is x^3, inner is -x^2. The order is everything — washer method demands outer minus inner. Dead on.

moves.name: V = π ∫_{-1}^{0} [(-x^2)^2 - (x^3)^2] dx
moves.professor: You reversed the radii. Outer minus inner, not the other way. That mistake turns your volume negative. The enemy exploited the opening.

moves.name: V = 2π ∫_{-1}^{0} x[(x^3) - (-x^2)] dx
moves.professor: That's a shell method setup — about the y-axis, not the x-axis. Wrong axis of rotation. You swung at a phantom.

questions.question: The graphs below intersect at three points, yet the area between them can be found by a single integral. Why?

moves.name: One function is always above the other on the interval
moves.professor: On [-1,1], 1-x² sits above (x²-1)² without crossing. A single top-minus-bottom integral sweeps the entire region. That's reading the battlefield correctly.

moves.name: The functions are symmetric about the y-axis
moves.professor: Symmetry alone doesn't guarantee a single integral — the upper and lower curves could still swap. You misjudged the terrain. The enemy struck.

moves.name: Three intersection points always require three separate integrals
moves.professor: Not always. Here the middle intersection is just a tangency, so the bounding curves never switch order. You abandoned the fight too early.

questions.question: The general solution y = C₁x + C₂x³ satisfies the differential equation. Which system of equations correctly determines the particular solution satisfying y(2)=0 and y'(2)=4?

moves.name: 2C₁ + 8C₂ = 0,  C₁ + 12C₂ = 4
moves.professor: y(2) = 2C₁ + 8C₂ = 0, and y' = C₁ + 3C₂x² gives y'(2) = C₁ + 12C₂ = 4. Both initial conditions hit dead center. Perfect aim.

moves.name: 2C₁ + 8C₂ = 4,  C₁ + 12C₂ = 0
moves.professor: You swapped the right-hand sides. The initial values landed on the wrong equations. A mix-up that cost you the kill.

moves.name: C₁ + C₂ = 0,  C₁ + 3C₂ = 4
moves.professor: You dropped the powers of 2 from the x terms. That's like forgetting the range on your weapon — the numbers don't match the actual solution structure.

questions.question: What is the most efficient method to evaluate this integral?

moves.name: Direct integration using the power rule
moves.professor: Three simple terms, all ready to integrate. No substitution needed. Walk up and strike.

moves.name: u-substitution with u = √x
moves.professor: You're overcomplicating a straight fight. The first term becomes 2/u but the others turn into a mess. The enemy gutted you while you fumbled.

moves.name: Integration by parts
moves.professor: There's no product of functions here. Parts is dead weight against this simple integrand. Wrong weapon, wrong fight.

questions.question: For the solid generated by revolving the region bounded by the curves below about y = π, which expression correctly gives the outer and inner radii for the washer method?

moves.name: Outer: π + x²,  Inner: π - x³
moves.professor: Distance from y=π to y=-x² is π + x²; to y=x³ is π - x³. Since x³ ≥ -x² on [-1,0], the outer radius is the larger distance. Bullseye.

moves.name: Outer: π - x³,  Inner: π + x²
moves.professor: You flipped inner and outer. The parabola is further from y=π than the cubic, so it's the outer radius. The enemy rolled right through that error.

moves.name: Outer: x³,  Inner: -x²
moves.professor: You forgot the axis is y=π, not y=0. Radii must be measured from the axis of rotation. You aimed at the wrong target entirely.

questions.question: To minimize the number of integrals needed, which variable of integration should be used for the area of the region R?

moves.name: Integrate with respect to y (one integral)
moves.professor: Horizontal slices span the whole region in one sweep. One integral, clean and efficient. You picked the right flank.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to x (one integral)
moves.professor: The curves cross in the x-direction — you'd need at least two integrals. A single x-integral misses the structure. The enemy dodged and struck back.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to x (two integrals)
moves.professor: That works, but it's the long route. Two integrals where one suffices. You got the kill, but you took the scenic path.

questions.question: Which first step correctly solves the differential equation?

moves.name: Separate: ∫ dy/(3+y)² = ∫ dx
moves.professor: The right side is a pure function of y. Cross-multiply and the variables split instantly. Separation is the blade for this fight.

moves.name: Multiply by integrating factor e^{∫ -2 dx}
moves.professor: Integrating factor is for linear equations. That squared term makes it nonlinear. You drew the wrong weapon from the arsenal.

moves.name: Integrate both sides directly: y = (3+y)² x + C
moves.professor: You treated (3+y)² as a constant with respect to y. It's not. That's a fundamental misunderstanding of what's being integrated.

questions.question: What is the best first step for evaluating this integral?

moves.name: Split into ∫ (x⁴ + 7/x) dx
moves.professor: Divide each term by x. Turns it into basic power rule pieces. No fancy footwork needed — just algebra.

moves.name: Let u = x⁵+7
moves.professor: Then du = 5x⁴ dx, and you don't have an x⁴ outside to absorb. The substitution doesn't match the battlefield. You got trapped.

moves.name: Use partial fraction decomposition
moves.professor: Partial fractions are for rational functions with factorable denominators. This denominator is just x. Massive overkill that leads nowhere.

questions.question: Using the method of cylindrical shells, set up the integral for the volume when the region under y = √x from x=0 to x=4 is revolved about the x-axis.

moves.name: 2π ∫₀² y(4 - y²) dy
moves.professor: Shells about the x-axis integrate with respect to y. Radius = y, height = 4 - y². The setup is flawless.

moves.name: 2π ∫₀⁴ x√x dx
moves.professor: That's shells about the y-axis, not the x-axis. You confused the axis of rotation and attacked the wrong flank.

moves.name: π ∫₀⁴ (√x)² dx
moves.professor: That's the disk method — which also gives the right volume for this axis. But the order was to use shells. You dodged the instruction but still hit the target.

questions.question: Which substitution simplifies this integral the fastest?

moves.name: u = x²
moves.professor: Then du = 2x dx, and the x in front is eaten perfectly. The exponential becomes eᵘ. Textbook kill.

moves.name: u = e^{x²}
moves.professor: Then du = 2x e^{x²} dx. You end up with the original integrand inside du, looping back on itself. A snake eating its own tail.

moves.name: Integration by parts with u = x, dv = e^{x²} dx
moves.professor: e^{x²} has no elementary antiderivative for dv. Parts crashes against that wall. You'd be swinging a wooden sword at stone.

questions.question: To find the area enclosed by the curves below, which variable of integration is more efficient?

moves.name: Integrate with respect to y
moves.professor: Both curves are solved for x. Right minus left gives a single y-integral. The path of least resistance.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to x (one integral)
moves.professor: Solving for y introduces ±√ terms and the region splits. A single x-integral won't cover it. You walked into an ambush.

moves.name: Integrate with respect to y (two integrals)
moves.professor: The region doesn't require splitting in y. You're making extra work for no reason. The enemy punished the hesitation.

questions.question: Set up the integral for the volume of the solid whose base is bounded by the curves below, with square cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis.

moves.name: ∫₋₁² [(x+1) - (x²-1)]² dx
moves.professor: Side length = top minus bottom. Square it for the area. Integrate across the intersection points x=-1,2. Clean geometry.

moves.name: ∫₋₁² [(x+1) - (x²-1)] dx
moves.professor: You forgot to square the side length. Area of a square is side². Without it, you're just integrating the base width. Half the weapon, no damage.

moves.name: π ∫₋₁² [(x+1)² - (x²-1)²] dx
moves.professor: That's the disk method for a solid of revolution. This solid has square cross-sections, not circular. Entirely wrong formation.

questions.question: Which first step correctly solves the differential equation?

moves.name: Separate: e^{-y} dy = x² dx, then integrate
moves.professor: Bring e^{-y} to the left, x² dx to the right. The variables split cleanly. A textbook strike.

moves.name: Use integrating factor e^{∫ x² dx}
moves.professor: This is nonlinear because of the e^y term. Integrating factors only work for linear first-order ODEs. You brought a shield to a sword fight and got overrun.

moves.name: Rewrite as dy/dx - x² e^y = 0 and apply exact methods
moves.professor: Technically it can be coerced into an exact form, but separation is far simpler. You're using a siege engine to swat a fly.

questions.question: A tank contains 200 lbs of salt in 1000 gal. Brine with 0.3 lbs/gal enters at 4 gal/min; the well-mixed solution drains at 2 gal/min. What type of differential equation models the amount of salt y(t)?

moves.name: Linear first-order
moves.professor: The volume increases, making the outflow term y-dependent but the equation is dy/dt + P(t)y = Q(t). An integrating factor will crack it. Correct read.

moves.name: Separable
moves.professor: The right side is a sum, not a product. You can't factor it as g(t)·h(y). The variables refuse to split. You charged an unbreakable line.

moves.name: Autonomous
moves.professor: The independent variable t appears explicitly in the outflow rate. Autonomous equations have no t on the right. This one does. Wrong classification.

questions.question: Using cylindrical shells, set up the integral for the volume when the region bounded by y=x, y=0, x=0, and x=4 is revolved about the line x=5.

moves.name: 2π ∫₀⁴ (5-x)x dx
moves.professor: Radius = 5-x, height = x. Shells parallel to x=5. All pieces in place — fire.

moves.name: 2π ∫₀⁴ (5-x) dx
moves.professor: You left out the height. Without the x, you're just sweeping circumferences. The volume is hollow. Enemy armor held.

moves.name: π ∫₀⁴ (5² - x²) dx
moves.professor: That's washers about the y-axis? No — the axis is vertical at x=5, not y=0. You deployed the wrong geometry entirely.

questions.question: Which substitution yields a simpler integral?

moves.name: u = 4+x
moves.professor: Linear shift. x = u-4 gives ∫(u-4)√u du. Expand and integrate. The fastest route to victory.

moves.name: u² = 4+x
moves.professor: Then x = u²-4, dx = 2u du. The integral becomes 2∫(u⁴ - 4u²) du. Heavier algebra, but the enemy still falls.

moves.name: u = x√(4+x)
moves.professor: Setting u to the whole integrand makes du a nightmare of product and chain rules. The weapon jammed immediately.

questions.question: Find all equilibrium solutions of the logistic model.

moves.name: P = 0 and P = N
moves.professor: Set dP/dt = 0. The product vanishes when P=0 or 1-P/N=0. Both are the stationary points. Identified and locked.

moves.name: P = k and P = N
moves.professor: k is the growth rate constant, not a population level. It drops out when you set the derivative to zero. You targeted a phantom.

moves.name: P = 0 only
moves.professor: You missed the carrying capacity N. That's a critical equilibrium. Incomplete reconnaissance got you hit.

questions.question: For a solid formed by rotating a region under a curve about the x-axis, cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are circular disks. Is this statement valid?

moves.name: True
moves.professor: Every slice perpendicular to the axis of revolution inherits the circular shape of the rotation. That's the geometry behind the disk method. Solid truth.

moves.name: False — they are washers, not disks
moves.professor: Washers appear only when there's a gap (hollow solid). A solid region under a single curve rotated gives full disks. You overthought and tripped.

moves.name: False — they are squares
moves.professor: Rotation generates circles, not squares. That's cross-sections of a different type of solid entirely. The enemy laughed at that one.

questions.question: What is the best first step for integrating this rational function?

moves.name: Perform polynomial long division
moves.professor: Degree of numerator equals denominator. Divide to get 1 + (x+1)/(x²+1). The remainder separates cleanly. Sliced through in one move.

moves.name: Apply partial fraction decomposition directly
moves.professor: Partial fractions require the numerator degree to be strictly less than the denominator. You didn't reduce first. The decomposition won't hold.

moves.name: Split as (x²+1 + x+1)/(x²+1), then separate
moves.professor: Clever: you added 1 in a smart way. That's essentially long division in disguise. Gets the job done, just a little unorthodox.
